title: Electronics Fundamentals Module 4: Diodes, LEDs, Zeners & Transistors (BJT/MOSFET)
overview: Covers PN junctions, forward voltage drops, bridge rectifiers, Zener regulation, and using transistors as switches/amplifiers.

1.label: Standard Diodes, Rectifiers & LEDs
1.what: A PN-junction one-way valve for electricity. Conducts easily when forward-biased (+ on Anode, - on Cathode/stripe) and blocks current when reverse-biased.
1.exam_facts: Silicon diode forward voltage drop (Vf) ≈ 0.7V (Germanium ≈ 0.3V). Full-Wave Bridge Rectifier uses 4 diodes to convert AC into pulsing DC. LEDs require a series current-limiting resistor: R = (Vs - Vf) / I.
1.troubleshoot: Use your DMM's Diode Test mode: Good silicon diode reads ~0.5V–0.7V one way and 'OL' (open) when you flip the leads. Reading 0.00V both ways = shorted diode!

2.label: Zener Diode (Voltage Regulation)
2.what: A special diode engineered to safely conduct backward (reverse breakdown) at a precise voltage, clamping output voltage steady.
2.exam_facts: Always installed in REVERSE bias (stripe/cathode toward positive) with a series resistor to absorb excess voltage. Used as a cheap voltage reference or over-voltage clamp.
2.troubleshoot: If Vout equals Vin instead of the Zener's rated voltage, either the Zener failed OPEN or it was accidentally installed backwards (acting like a 0.7V standard diode).

3.label: BJT Transistor (NPN / PNP - Current Controlled)
3.what: A 3-pin semiconductor (Base, Collector, Emitter) where a tiny current into the Base controls a much larger current flowing from Collector to Emitter.
3.exam_facts: Current Gain = Beta (β or hFE) = Ic / Ib. In NPN, 'Not Pointing iN' (arrow points out on Emitter); Base must be ~0.7V higher than Emitter to turn ON (Saturation).
3.troubleshoot: Always put a resistor (e.g., 1kΩ) in series with the Base pin—connecting a microcontroller pin straight to a BJT Base without a resistor acts like a dead short through the 0.7V junction!

4.label: MOSFET (Voltage Controlled Power Switch)
4.what: Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor (Gate, Drain, Source). Uses an electric field (voltage on Gate) instead of continuous current to switch heavy loads.
4.exam_facts: Extremely high input impedance on the Gate (draws almost zero steady current). Very low on-resistance (Rds(on)), so MOSFETs run much cooler than BJTs when switching motors or high-current LEDs.
4.troubleshoot: MOSFET gates are super sensitive to static (ESD) and shouldn't be left 'floating'—always add a 10kΩ pull-down resistor from Gate to Source so noise doesn't randomly turn your load on.
